pos: adj. (owing a debt; under obligation to another)
etymology: From in- + debt, through Old French dette from Latin debitum, a thing owed, the past participle of debere, to owe. The silent b was restored by scholars to show the Latin root.
biblical_def: The word stands once in the Authorized Version, inside the prayer the Lord taught His disciples: “And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us.” Luke renders the first petition as sins and the second as indebted, so that the two words interpret one another. Sin is a debt owed to God, a debt of perfect obedience that no son of Adam has paid and none can pay. The one who has been forgiven that infinite debt is therefore bound to release the lesser debts others owe him. This is not a bargain by which our forgiving purchases God's forgiving; the parable of the unmerciful servant (Matthew 18) shows the order plainly, for the king forgives first, and the servant's cruelty afterward proves that the mercy never took hold of his heart. The forgiven forgive. To pray this clause honestly a man must remember that he stands before God far more deeply indebted than any man stands before him, and that every debt of the elect was paid in full at the cross, where Christ bore the reckoning of His people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): INDEBTED, being in debt; having incurred a debt; held to payment or requital; obliged by something received.
webster_full: INDEBTED, a. Being in debt; having incurred a debt; held to payment or requital.
Obliged by something received, for which restitution or gratitude is due; as, we are indebted to our parents for their care.
Luke 11:4 sets indebted beside sins in the Lord's Prayer, so that each word explains the other.
Sin is pictured as a debt owed to God which the sinner cannot discharge.
The forgiven debtor is bound to release the debts owed to him.
scriptures: Luk 11:4
And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation; but deliver us from evil.
Mat 6:12
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
Then the lord of that servant was moved with compassion, and loosed him, and forgave him the debt.
corruption_summary: The prayer is bent into a transaction, as though our forgiving others earns God's forgiveness, or emptied into a therapeutic release of grudges for our own peace rather than obedience flowing from a debt already cancelled.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors pull at this clause. The first reads it as a condition of merit: forgive enough and God will forgive you. That reverses the gospel order, for God forgives the elect freely in Christ and the forgiving spirit is the fruit, not the price, of that pardon. The second, more modern, strips God out entirely and treats forgiveness as a self-care technique, releasing resentment because it is bad for the one who holds it.

Scripture keeps the vertical debt first. The sinner is indebted to God beyond all reckoning; Christ paid the debt; and the man who knows himself so forgiven cannot hold his brother by the throat over a hundred pence (Matthew 18:28). Forgiveness of others is obedience and gratitude, not therapy and not merit.
roots_summary: From Latin debitum, a thing owed; Luke 11:4 places indebted beside sins in the Lord's Prayer.
roots_lines: Latin debere, to owe; debitum, a thing owed.
Old French dette gave English debt; indebted means under that obligation.
Luke 11:4 is the only use in the Authorized Version.
Matthew 6:12 gives the parallel petition in the language of debts and debtors.
Matthew 18 shows the forgiven servant bound to forgive his fellow.
usage: for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us
pictures sin as a debt the sinner owes God and cannot pay
binds the forgiven to release what others owe them

pos: v. (past participle; pledged land or goods as security for a debt)
etymology: From Old French mort gage, literally “dead pledge”: mort, dead, from Latin mortuus, and gage, a pledge. The pledge was called dead because it was lost to the debtor if he failed to pay.
biblical_def: In the days of Nehemiah the walls of Jerusalem were rising, but inside them the people were sinking. “Some also there were that said, We have mortgaged our lands, vineyards, and houses, that we might buy corn, because of the dearth.” Famine had driven the poor to pledge their inheritance, and the richer Jews had taken the pledges and were exacting usury from their own brethren, until sons and daughters were being sold into bondage (Nehemiah 5:5). Nehemiah's anger was holy anger: the law of Moses forbade lending upon usury to a brother (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:36-37), and the land itself belonged to the LORD and was never to be sold forever (Leviticus 25:23). He rebuked the nobles, called a great assembly, and made them restore the fields, vineyards, oliveyards and houses that same day (Nehemiah 5:11). The rebuilding of the city was hollow while the covenant brotherhood within it was being foreclosed. The word stands as a warning that outward work for God does not excuse grinding the faces of the poor within the household of faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): MORTGAGE, to grant or convey an estate in fee as security for the payment of money; to pledge.
webster_full: MORTGAGE, v.t. To grant an estate in fee as security for money lent, the estate to be void on payment of the debt.
To pledge; to make liable to the payment of any debt or expenditure.
Nehemiah 5:3 records the poor of Judah mortgaging lands, vineyards and houses in a famine.
Their brethren exacted usury from them, contrary to the law of Moses.
Nehemiah compelled the restoration of the pledged property.
scriptures: Neh 5:3
Some also there were that said, We have mortgaged our lands, vineyards, and houses, that we might buy corn, because of the dearth.
Neh 5:11

Restore, I pray you, to them, even this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards, and their houses, also the hundredth part of the money, and of the corn, the wine, and the oil, that ye exact of them.
Take thou no usury of him, or increase: but fear thy God; that thy brother may live with thee.
corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition attaches to the word; the live danger is a church busy with building projects while the debts and needs of its own poor go unregarded.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word keeps its plain commercial sense.

The principle to recover is Nehemiah's: covenant brotherhood governs how believers deal with one another's money. Lending is not forbidden, but exploiting a brother's extremity is, and no zeal for walls and works can cover it. Deacons, elders and households are still called to see that the poor of the congregation are not ground down while the visible work goes forward.
roots_summary: Old French mort gage, a dead pledge; Nehemiah 5:3 records the poor mortgaging their inheritance in famine.
roots_lines: Mort, dead, and gage, pledge, from Old French.
The pledge was dead to the debtor if he failed to pay.
Nehemiah 5:3 is the only occurrence in the Authorized Version.
Leviticus 25:36 forbids taking usury of a poor brother.
Nehemiah 5:11 commands the restoration of the pledged fields and houses.
usage: we have mortgaged our lands, vineyards, and houses
records the poor of Judah pledging their inheritance in famine
warns against exploiting a brother's extremity

pos: v. (past participle; lost or surrendered as a penalty)
etymology: From Old French forfait, a crime or transgression, from Medieval Latin forisfactum, a thing done outside (foris) the law. What was forfeited was the penalty that followed the transgression. The translators' margin gives the Hebrew sense: devoted.
biblical_def: When Ezra learned that the returned exiles, priests and Levites among them, had taken wives of the peoples of the land, he rent his garment and sat astonied until the evening sacrifice. The congregation answered with a proclamation: whoever would not come to Jerusalem within three days, “all his substance should be forfeited, and himself separated from the congregation of those that had been carried away.” The Hebrew word behind forfeited is the word for the ban, the thing devoted to God and removed from common use, the same word used of Jericho. The penalty was severe because the danger was severe: the remnant had gone into captivity precisely for mingling with the nations and their gods, and to repeat that sin within a generation of the return was to court the same judgment. The proclamation teaches that the purity of the covenant people is worth costly discipline. The church today does not confiscate goods, for it bears the keys and not the sword, but it still must separate from its fellowship those who refuse to repent, for the sake of their souls and the holiness of Christ's house.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FORFEIT, lost or alienated by an offense, crime, or breach of condition; FORFEITED, lost by breach of condition.
webster_full: FORFEIT, n. That which is forfeited or lost, or the right to which is alienated by a crime, offense, neglect of duty, or breach of contract.
FORFEIT, v.t. To lose or render confiscable by some fault, offense or crime.
Ezra 10:8 threatens that the substance of those who refuse the assembly shall be forfeited.
The margin renders the Hebrew devoted, the language of the ban.
The penalty guarded the returned remnant from repeating the sin that sent Israel into exile.
scriptures: Ezr 10:8

And that whosoever would not come within three days, according to the counsel of the princes and the elders, all his substance should be forfeited, and himself separated from the congregation of those that had been carried away.
Ezr 9:2

For they have taken of their daughters for themselves, and for their sons: so that the holy seed have mingled themselves with the people of those lands: yea, the hand of the princes and rulers hath been chief in this trespass.
But them that are without God judgeth. Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person.
corruption_summary: Church discipline is treated as unloving exclusion, so that congregations forfeit holiness itself rather than ever separating the impenitent.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct recoils at any penalty for refusing the assembly's judgment. Discipline is called judgmental, separation is called exclusion, and the only sin left is the sin of naming sin. Under that pressure many churches have abandoned the third mark of a true church, the right exercise of discipline, which the Reformers set beside the preaching of the Word and the right administration of the ordinances.

Ezra's assembly shows that the people of God are a holy people with boundaries. Christ gave His church the keys (Matthew 18:17-18), and Paul commands, “put away from among yourselves that wicked person” (1 Corinthians 5:13). Rightly used, discipline is mercy: it warns the sinner while there is time and keeps the flock from leaven.
roots_summary: Latin forisfactum, a thing done outside the law; Ezra 10:8 uses forfeited for the devoted substance of those who refused the assembly.
roots_lines: Medieval Latin forisfactum, a deed outside the law.
Old French forfait, a transgression and its penalty.
Ezra 10:8 is the only occurrence in the Authorized Version.
The margin reads devoted, the Hebrew word of the ban.
The penalty guarded the remnant from mingling with the nations.
usage: all his substance should be forfeited
names the penalty laid on those who refused Ezra's assembly
underlines the costly discipline that guards the covenant people

pos: v. (past participle; freed from an obligation that binds others)
etymology: From Latin exemptus, past participle of eximere, to take out, from ex, out, and emere, to take. The translators' margin gives the Hebrew as simply free.
biblical_def: Baasha king of Israel had fortified Ramah to choke the road into Judah. When the threat lifted, King Asa summoned the whole kingdom: “Then king Asa made a proclamation throughout all Judah; none was exempted: and they took away the stones of Ramah, and the timber thereof, wherewith Baasha had builded; and king Asa built with them Geba of Benjamin, and Mizpah.” Every hand was called to the work, and the enemy's own building materials became the walls of Judah's defence. The phrase none was exempted is a small window onto a large truth: in the common labour of God's people no one stands outside the call. Yet the account is tinged with sorrow, for Asa had bought this relief by stripping the treasuries of the temple to hire Ben-hadad of Syria (1 Kings 15:18-19), and the prophet Hanani later rebuked him for relying on the king of Syria and not on the LORD (2 Chronicles 16:7). The universal summons was right; the alliance that made it possible was faithless. The people of God are all enlisted, but their strength must be the LORD, not the wealth of the house of God traded for the help of man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): EXEMPT, free from any service, charge, burden, tax, duty, evil or requisition to which others are subject; EXEMPTED, freed from.
webster_full: EXEMPT, v.t. To take out or from; to free or permit to be free from any charge, burden, restraint, duty, evil or requisition.
EXEMPT, a. Free by privilege; not subject; not liable to.
1 Kings 15:22 records Asa's proclamation in which none in Judah was exempted.
The stones and timber of Baasha's fort at Ramah were carried away to build Geba and Mizpah.
The margin gives the Hebrew sense as free.
scriptures: Then king Asa made a proclamation throughout all Judah; none was exempted: and they took away the stones of Ramah, and the timber thereof, wherewith Baasha had builded; and king Asa built with them Geba of Benjamin, and Mizpah.

Then Asa took all the silver and the gold that were left in the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king's house, and delivered them into the hand of his servants: and king Asa sent them to Benhadad, the son of Tabrimon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, that dwelt at Damascus, saying,

And at that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah, and said unto him, Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand.
corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is that no member of the covenant people is exempt from the common labour, and no labour excuses trusting man rather than God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word keeps its plain legal sense.

Two lessons are worth recovering. Every member of Christ's body has a part to bear, and the consumer habit of treating church as a service received rather than a work shared is foreign to the summons Asa issued. And no outward success excuses the faithless means used to obtain it; Asa's alliance with Syria is recorded with the prophet's rebuke beside it.
roots_summary: Latin eximere, to take out; 1 Kings 15:22 records that none in Judah was exempted from Asa's summons.
roots_lines: Latin ex, out, and emere, to take.
Exemptus, taken out, freed from an obligation.
1 Kings 15:22 is the only occurrence in the Authorized Version.
The margin renders the Hebrew simply free.
Hanani's rebuke in 2 Chronicles 16:7 shadows Asa's success.
usage: none was exempted
records the whole of Judah summoned to dismantle Baasha's fort
teaches that every member of the covenant people shares the common work

pos: n. (that which remains beyond a reckoned amount; surplus)
etymology: A half-translation of Old French surplus: English over joined to Latin plus, more. The word names whatever is left over after the account is reckoned.
biblical_def: The law of redemption in Leviticus 25 protected the inheritance of every Israelite family. A man driven by poverty to sell his land did not sell it forever; he sold only the harvests until the jubilee. If he later prospered and could redeem it himself, “Then let him count the years of the sale thereof, and restore the overplus unto the man to whom he sold it; that he may return unto his possession.” The price was reckoned by the years remaining; the buyer received back only the overplus, the value of the harvests he had not yet enjoyed, and the land returned to its family. The arithmetic is plain, but the theology is deep. “The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine” (Leviticus 25:23). Every transaction in Israel was bounded by the LORD's ownership and His jubilee. The law points beyond itself to the Kinsman-Redeemer who restores to His people the inheritance they lost, not by paying a reckoned overplus but by paying the whole price in His own blood, so that they return to their possession forever.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): OVERPLUS, surplus; that which remains after a supply, or beyond a quantity proposed.
webster_full: OVERPLUS, n. Surplus; that which remains after a supply, or beyond a quantity proposed.
Leviticus 25:27 uses the word for the balance the redeemer of land pays back to the buyer.
The price was reckoned by the years remaining until the jubilee.
The law kept every family's inheritance from being sold forever.
The pattern foreshadows Christ the Kinsman-Redeemer.
scriptures: Then let him count the years of the sale thereof, and restore the overplus unto the man to whom he sold it; that he may return unto his possession.
And in all the land of your possession ye shall grant a redemption for the land.
If thy brother be waxen poor, and hath sold away some of his possession, and if any of his kin come to redeem it, then shall he redeem that which his brother sold.
corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is that all property is held under God's ownership and bounded by His law of mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word survives in plain commercial use.

What is worth recovering is the frame around the arithmetic. Modern economies treat ownership as absolute and reckon every bargain by the market alone; Leviticus reckons every bargain under the LORD who says the land is His. Believers hold what they own as stewards, and deal with the poor under a law that remembers they too were redeemed.
roots_summary: English over plus Latin plus, more; Leviticus 25:27 names the balance restored when land is redeemed before the jubilee.
roots_lines: Half-translation of Old French surplus.
English over with Latin plus, more.
Leviticus 25:27 is the only occurrence in the Authorized Version.
Leviticus 25:24 grants a redemption for all the land of Israel's possession.
Christ the Kinsman-Redeemer restores the lost inheritance in full.
usage: restore the overplus unto the man to whom he sold it
names the balance paid back when land was redeemed
rests on the LORD's declaration that the land is His

pos: v.t. (archaic; to bring loss or damage upon)
etymology: From en-, to cause, and damage, from Old French damage, from Latin damnum, loss or hurt. An older, fuller form of the verb damage.
biblical_def: When the returned exiles began rebuilding Jerusalem, their adversaries wrote to Artaxerxes king of Persia. Their letter was a masterpiece of slander dressed as loyalty: “Be it known now unto the king, that, if this city be builded, and the walls set up again, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings.” They cast the people of God as a rebellious and bad city and warned that the treasury would suffer. The charge succeeded; the king ordered the work to cease, and it stopped until the second year of Darius (Ezra 4:24). The enemies of God's work rarely attack it on its true ground. They do not confess their hatred of the God of Israel; they say the work will endamage the revenue, threaten order, or disturb the peace. Yet the work that was stopped by a letter was resumed by a prophet, for Haggai and Zechariah stirred the people to build again (Ezra 5:1-2), and what God had purposed the kings of Persia could delay but not destroy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ENDAMAGE, to bring loss or damage to; to harm; to injure; to mischief.
webster_full: ENDAMAGE, v.t. To bring loss or damage to; to harm; to injure; to mischief; to prejudice.
The word is nearly superseded by damage.
Ezra 4:13 records the adversaries' warning that the rebuilt city would endamage the revenue of the kings.
The charge persuaded Artaxerxes to halt the work.
The prophets Haggai and Zechariah stirred the people to resume building.
scriptures: Ezr 4:13
Be it known now unto the king, that, if this city be builded, and the walls set up again, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings.
Ezr 4:24
Then ceased the work of the house of God which is at Jerusalem. So it ceased unto the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.
Ezr 5:1
Then the prophets, Haggai the prophet, and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied unto the Jews that were in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel, even unto them.
corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is that the enemies of God's work commonly disguise hostility to God as concern for revenue, order or public peace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is simply archaic.

The pattern it records is perennial. Faithful churches are opposed in the language of civic harm: their teaching is said to endanger, their gatherings to disturb, their convictions to cost the community. Believers should answer as Ezra's generation finally did, by continuing the work God commanded, appealing to lawful authority where they can and fearing God rather than man.

roots_lines: Latin damnum, loss or hurt, gave Old French damage.
The prefix en- makes the verb: to bring damage upon.
Ezra 4:13 is the only occurrence in the Authorized Version.
The slander halted the rebuilding until the reign of Darius.

pos: adj. (short of the full or proper amount)
etymology: From Old Norse skamt, the neuter of skammr, short. In English it came to describe whatever is measured short of what is due.
biblical_def: Micah's indictment of Jerusalem reaches into the marketplace: “Are there yet the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure that is abominable?” The scant measure was the ephah cut short, the basket that held less than it claimed, so that the buyer paid for a full measure and carried home a short one. The LORD does not call it shrewd business; He calls it abominable, the same word used of idolatry. The law had commanded just balances and a just ephah (Leviticus 19:36), and Proverbs had said that “a false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight” (Proverbs 11:1). The reason is that God is Himself perfectly just, and every short measure is a lie told with the hands. Micah follows the question with the verdict: “Therefore also will I make thee sick in smiting thee” (Micah 6:13). The same God who requires that men do justly, love mercy and walk humbly with Him (Micah 6:8) weighs the merchant's ephah.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SCANT, not full, large or plentiful; scarcely sufficient; less than is wanted for the purpose.
webster_full: SCANT, a. Not full, large or plentiful; scarcely sufficient; rather less than is wanted for the purpose.
Sparing; parsimonious; cautiously affording.
Micah 6:10 calls the scant measure abominable.
The law required a just ephah and just balances (Leviticus 19:36).
A margin note at 2 Kings 4:3 also renders borrow not a few as scant not.
scriptures: Mic 6:10
Are there yet the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure that is abominable?
Mic 6:11
Shall I count them pure with the wicked balances, and with the bag of deceitful weights?
Pro 11:1
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
corruption_summary: Commerce is treated as morally neutral, so that shaving the measure, hiding the fee or shrinking the product passes as clever business rather than an abomination before God.
corruption_paragraphs: The ancient scant measure has modern descendants: the package that shrinks while the price holds, the fee buried in fine print, the hour billed but not worked. A culture that judges business only by profit and legality has no category for calling these things abominable.

Scripture does. The just God requires just measure, and He reckons the short ephah among the sins that bring His judgment on a city. Christian workers, merchants and employers are bound to give full measure because they serve a Master in heaven (Colossians 4:1).
roots_summary: Old Norse skammr, short; Micah 6:10 condemns the scant measure as abominable.
roots_lines: Old Norse skamt, short, gave English scant.
The word describes what is measured short of what is due.
Micah 6:10 is the only use in the text of the Authorized Version.
The law required a just ephah (Leviticus 19:36).
Proverbs 11:1 calls the false balance an abomination to the LORD.
usage: the scant measure that is abominable
condemns the short ephah of dishonest trade

pos: v.t. (to bring legal action against; to prosecute a claim at law)
etymology: From Anglo-French suer, Old French sivre, to follow, from Latin sequi, to follow. To sue was first to follow after a claim, and so to pursue it in court.
biblical_def: In the Sermon on the Mount the Lord takes up the law of retaliation and lays a deeper claim on His disciples: “And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also.” The coat was the inner garment, the cloke the outer one that the law protected even from a creditor (Exodus 22:26-27). Christ teaches that His people should be willing to yield even what the law would let them keep, rather than return evil for evil. This is not a command abolishing courts or forbidding a magistrate to do justice; Paul himself appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11). It is a command against the vengeful spirit that grasps for every right and treats the law as a weapon of retaliation. Paul applies the same principle to the church: “Why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?” (1 Corinthians 6:7). The disciple who has been forgiven an infinite debt and who looks for an inheritance incorruptible can afford to lose a cloke.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SUE, to seek justice or right from one by legal process; to prosecute in a civil action for the recovery of a real or supposed right.
webster_full: SUE, v.t. To seek justice or right from one by legal process; to commence a civil action against.
To gain by legal process. To clean the beak, as a hawk (obsolete sense).
SUE, v.i. To prosecute; to make legal claim; to seek for in law.
Matthew 5:40 commands yielding the cloke to one who sues for the coat.
The teaching forbids a retaliating spirit, not lawful justice.
scriptures: Mat 5:40
And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also.
Mat 5:39
But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.
Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?
corruption_summary: The text is twisted two ways: into a pacifist denial that civil justice may ever be sought, or, far more commonly, ignored altogether by believers who sue and are sued as freely as the world.
corruption_paragraphs: Some read Matthew 5:40 as abolishing all recourse to law and all use of force by the magistrate. That ignores Romans 13, where the ruler is God's minister bearing the sword, and Paul's own appeals to Roman justice. The Sermon on the Mount governs the disciple's personal spirit, not the office of the civil ruler.

The more common corruption is simple neglect. Believers litigate against one another as readily as unbelievers, and 1 Corinthians 6 is passed over. Christ's word calls His people to a holy willingness to suffer loss, and the church to settle disputes among brethren before the world's tribunals are ever involved.
roots_summary: Latin sequi, to follow; Matthew 5:40 commands yielding the cloke to one who sues for the coat.
roots_lines: Latin sequi, to follow, through Old French sivre.
To sue was to follow after a claim in court.
Matthew 5:40 is the only occurrence in the Authorized Version.
The cloke was protected by the law of Exodus 22:26-27.
1 Corinthians 6:7 applies the same spirit within the church.
usage: if any man will sue thee at the law
commands a disciple to yield rather than retaliate
governs personal spirit without abolishing the magistrate's justice

pos: v. (past participle; carried over from one person or thing to another)
etymology: From Latin transferre, to carry across, from trans, across, and ferre, to bear. The Greek word Paul uses, metaschematizo, means to change the outward form of a thing.
biblical_def: The Corinthians had split into parties around their teachers: “I am of Paul; and I of Apollos.” Paul spent three chapters dismantling the boast, and then explained his method: “And these things, brethren, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos for your sakes; that ye might learn in us not to think of men above that which is written, that no one of you be puffed up for one against another.” He had applied the argument to himself and Apollos as an illustration, so that no living faction leader in Corinth would be named, and yet every faction would see itself. The lesson he drew is a rule for the whole church: not to think of men above that which is written. Preachers are servants and stewards (1 Corinthians 4:1); their gifts are received, not owned (4:7); and to glory in a man is to forget that all things are the church's because the church is Christ's (3:21-23). The verse also teaches that Scripture is the measure of every minister, and that party spirit around celebrated teachers is a form of pride.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): TRANSFER, to convey from one place or person to another; to transport; to make over the possession or control of.
webster_full: TRANSFER, v.t. To convey from one place or person to another; to transport or remove to another place or person.
To make over the possession or control of; to pass, as a title or right.
1 Corinthians 4:6 uses transferred of Paul applying his argument to himself and Apollos as a figure.
The purpose was that the Corinthians not think of men above that which is written.
The verse rebukes party spirit gathered around teachers.
scriptures: And these things, brethren, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos for your sakes; that ye might learn in us not to think of men above that which is written, that no one of you be puffed up for one against another.
For while one saith, I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos; are ye not carnal?
Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God.
corruption_summary: The celebrity culture of modern evangelicalism repeats Corinth's error, ranking and following teachers as brands and thinking of men above what is written.
corruption_paragraphs: Corinth's factions have modern descendants in conference platforms, follower counts and tribes named after favourite preachers. The man becomes the measure, and Scripture is read through him rather than he through Scripture.

Paul's rule cuts through all of it: not to think of men above that which is written. Ministers are stewards to be found faithful, and the only authority that binds the conscience is the Word they serve. Believers honour faithful teachers, but they belong to Christ, not to Paul, Apollos or any modern name.

pos: adj. (not weighed; left without being measured by weight)
etymology: From un-, not, and weighed, from Old English wegan, to carry, lift or weigh. The margin gives the Hebrew reason: “for the exceeding multitude.”
biblical_def: When Hiram of Tyre had finished the brass work for Solomon's temple, the pillars Jachin and Boaz, the molten sea, the bases, lavers, pots, shovels and basons, the record closes with a remarkable line: “And Solomon left all the vessels unweighed, because they were exceeding many: neither was the weight of the brass found out.” In a world where every precious metal was carefully weighed, here was abundance beyond the scales. David had prepared “brass in abundance without weight” (1 Chronicles 22:3, 14), and Solomon's craftsmen poured out more than could be reckoned. The house built for the name of the LORD was furnished with a lavishness that refused to count the cost. The detail is a picture of the glory of God's dwelling, which in its fulfilment is no house of brass but Christ Himself and His church. The riches of His grace are likewise unweighed; Paul calls them “the unsearchable riches of Christ” (Ephesians 3:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): UNWEIGHED, not weighed; having the weight not ascertained; not deliberately considered.
webster_full: UNWEIGHED, a. Not weighed; having the weight not ascertained.
Not deliberately considered and examined; as, words unweighed.

corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is the lavish devotion that refuses to count the cost of what is given for the worship of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word keeps its plain sense.

The temple's unweighed brass rebukes a grudging spirit that gives to God only what is left over and calculates the minimum. The new covenant does not call for brass, but it calls for the cheerful giving of believers who have received grace without measure (2 Corinthians 9:7).
